How does Canonical work?

The Rust source code can be difficult to understand.

Introducing Canonical-min, a sound and complete automated theorem prover for dependent type theory, written in only 185 lines of Lean code.

The accompanying preprint explains the entire implementation line-by-line, assuming no prior knowledge of dependent type theory. Canonical-min serves as a simplified reference for the algorithm behind Canonical, and a baseline for the development of future automated reasoning tools. A special feature of this implementation is the use of the continuation monad to convert the type checker into a constraint solver.
We compare Canonical-min against other (incomplete) type inhabitation systems in Rocq, Agda, and Twelf, using our new benchmark DTTBench. We hope Canonical-min can help drive forward the development of general automation for proof assistants.

I think this is nice, but I’m convinced the biggest thing preventing wider adoption of Canonical by mathematicians is that Mathlib doesn’t not depend on it. This is the fate of any automation that is not available by default. Every mathlib user can try grind because you type grind and it just works. Nobody uses duper or the Lean hammer or canonical because when you open a Mathlib file and type duper or canonical nothing happens. Note I have no idea whether people doing programming or software verification are using those tools.
Can canonical-min be used as a subroutine in other tactics? Are there current tactics that could benefit from this?
If lake had dev dependencies then making Mathlib depend on it would be less of an issue.

Jireh Loreaux said:

If lake had dev dependencies then making Mathlib depend on it would be less of an issue.

What is the difference in this case? Wouldn’t downstream users want canonical as well?

#30953 adds Canonical, but AFAIK the issue is that we can't just add any potential cool new tactic to Mathlib, rather we should find a way to let anyone add local dependencies (without invalidating Mathlib's cache).

I think adding a "preamble" to the LSP would be nice to e.g. make the LSP prepend import Canonical to every file opened but without affecting lake build.
That way one could try using canonical without having to add the import to Mathlib.Init which would invalidate the cache and require a local rebuild.

If I understand correctly, the purpose of canonical-min is not to make the tactic canonical more accessible to mathlib contributors (which would require following Patrick Massot's suggestion); rather, it is to make the type theory more accessible to those who want to build on it. Canonical is a really cool type theory (the syntax is designed in such a way to mean that all expressions are already normalized, and it is extremely high performance) so there's a lot of potential for more complicated tactics built on top of it. Also, if I remember correctly, one of the eventual goals was to formalize the metatheory of canonical in Lean.

Shreyas Srinivas said:

Jireh Loreaux said:

If lake had dev dependencies then making Mathlib depend on it would be less of an issue.

What is the difference in this case? Wouldn’t downstream users want canonical as well?

The difference is just exposure. Mathlib would be more willing to adopt (some) dependencies if they are useful, but right now it means we also force everyone downstream to depend on it. But if its in Mathlib as a dev dependency, then people can use it when hacking on Mathlib, and then they'll be more likely to want to add it to their projects downstream.

@Patrick Massot Canonical-min is not intended to increase the adoption of Canonical, but rather to provide a reference implementation for those interested in automated theorem proving. @Niels Voss has it correct

@Shreyas Srinivas canonical can already be used as a subroutine when imported, see Canonical/Main.lean. You can use Canonical-min as a subroutine, too, but it is less efficient and has fewer features than Canonical.

@Snir Broshi There is no such issue with adding Canonical to Mathlib. All that needs to be done is add behavior to lake exe cache get which fetches the build archive for Canonical (see thread). Canonical is unique in that it strictly requires the build archive (as it contains the Rust dynlib).

The cache of Canonical itself is not the issue I was talking about. If a user locally adds import Canonical to Mathlib/Init.lean, there's no fix you can make to lake exe cache get that'll help avoid a rebuild of Mathlib.

Jireh Loreaux said:

Shreyas Srinivas said:

Jireh Loreaux said:

If lake had dev dependencies then making Mathlib depend on it would be less of an issue.

What is the difference in this case? Wouldn’t downstream users want canonical as well?

The difference is just exposure. Mathlib would be more willing to adopt (some) dependencies if they are useful, but right now it means we also force everyone downstream to depend on it. But if its in Mathlib as a dev dependency, then people can use it when hacking on Mathlib, and then they'll be more likely to want to add it to their projects downstream.

I don't think this describes any traditional meaning of a dev dependency, which would be something that assists in but cannot be part of the actual build of Mathlib. Perhaps a concept of "private dependency" that is able to provide tactics actually usable in code to be committed but cannot be public imported and so is not visible to downstream packages (unless they do import all...) would be a better fit here?
Sebastian, canonical is a self-replacing tactic, it never appears anywhere in committed code.
Also isn’t making canonical available to downstream users part of the goal here?
As I said above, the point would be exposure.
